text:
American Airlines and Infinium have announced the first delivery of electro sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF) to a commercial airport for use on a commercial passenger flight, in what the companies describe as a major milestone in aviation decarbonization.

The eSAF was allocated to an American Airlines flight that departed Corpus Christi International Airport (CRP) and landed at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW). The fuel was produced and blended at Infinium’s Pathfinder facility in Corpus Christi – described as the world’s first commercial-scale power-to-liquids e-fuels production site, operating since 2023 – and blended with conventional jet fuel to meet the ASTM International specification for Jet A, certifying its use in current aircraft engines and fueling infrastructure without modification. The companies said it marked the first delivery of SAF made without biobased feedstocks to a commercial US airport.

Infinium’s eSAF is produced using waste CO2 and renewable electricity, and the company says it can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by more than 90% compared with conventional petroleum-based jet fuel.

Robert Schuetzle, CEO of Infinium, said, “Since 2023, we have been producing scalable, drop-in eDiesel and eNaphtha at our Pathfinder facility from waste carbon and renewable energy for use in commercial trucks and plastics processing. Adding eSAF to our product slate – and seeing it power a commercial passenger flight – marks another meaningful step forward in bringing practical, low-carbon fuel solutions to industry.”

American has an offtake agreement for commercial volumes of eSAF from Infinium’s Project Roadrunner, financed by Breakthrough Energy Catalyst and Brookfield Asset Management with nonrecourse project debt from HSBC. The project is under construction and expected to begin eSAF production and deliveries in 2027, with capacity to produce more than five million gallons of eSAF annually once fully operational.

Robert Isom, American Airline’s CEO, said, “This flight represents a significant moment for aviation. Through our partnership with Infinium, we’re demonstrating how next generation technologies like eSAF can move from early investment to real-world application.”

Aviation currently consumes nearly 100 billion gallons of jet fuel annually, with sustainable aviation fuel accounting for less than 1% of total global jet fuel use, according to the companies.

title: Aviation minister rejects claims of ethanol blending in jet fuel - BioEnergy Times
description:

He said SAF is an internationally certified aviation fuel recognised by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and is already being adopted globally.
According to the minister, SAF undergoes rigorous testing and complies with stringent international safety standards before being approved for aviation use.
Aviation experts also said ethanol cannot simply be blended with aviation turbine fuel because of technical and chemical compatibility issues.
Sustainable Aviation Fuel is produced from renewable feedstocks and can reduce lifecycle carbon dioxide emissions by 65% to 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.
text:
New Delhi: Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu on Thursday dismissed claims that the Centre was planning to blend ethanol with Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF), calling the allegations “completely false and irresponsible.”

In a post on social media platform X, Naidu said there was no proposal to blend ethanol with aviation fuel and warned that spreading misinformation about aviation safety could create unnecessary anxiety among air travellers, The New Indian Express reported.

“There is no such proposal. Spreading misinformation on aviation safety only creates needless anxiety among air travellers,” the minister said, adding that passenger safety remains the government’s highest priority.

Naidu’s remarks came in response to allegations made by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) national convener Arvind Kejriwal, who claimed the Centre was considering ethanol blending in ATF and questioned the safety of such a move.

Clarifying the issue, the minister said ethanol and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) are entirely different fuels and should not be confused.

He said SAF is an internationally certified aviation fuel recognised by the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) and is already being adopted globally. According to the minister, SAF undergoes rigorous testing and complies with stringent international safety standards before being approved for aviation use.

Aviation experts also said ethanol cannot simply be blended with aviation turbine fuel because of technical and chemical compatibility issues. They noted that while ethanol is commonly blended with petrol, it is not compatible with diesel or conventional jet fuel without extensive scientific evaluation.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel is produced from renewable feedstocks and can reduce lifecycle carbon dioxide emissions by 65% to 80% compared with conventional jet fuel.

The International Civil Aviation Organization has identified SAF as the most effective pathway for achieving the aviation sector’s goal of net-zero carbon emissions by 2050 and is supporting member countries in expanding its production and use through training and technical assistance.

title: What does a Burnham government mean for UK aerospace? - Royal Aeronautical Society
description:

References 1] https://www.adsadvance.co.uk/prime-minister-andy-burnham-message-to-farnborough-airshow/ 2] https://www.adsgroup.org.uk/knowledge/value-of-aerospace-defence-security-and-space-to-the-uk-grew-two-thirds-since-2015-ads-finds/ 3] https://www.gov.uk/government/news/business-secretary-im-backing-investment-and-innovation-to-power-good-growth-in-every-corner-of-the-uk 4] https://www.gov.uk/government/organisations/department-for-business-and-trade 5] https://www.johnhealeymp.co.uk/john-healey-unveils-transformational-defence-investment/ 6] https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-defence-investment-plan/the-defence-investment-plan-funding-explainer 7] https://www.gov.uk/government/news/uk-drone-transformation-to-strengthen-armed-forces-backed-by-more-than-5-billion 8] https://www.forcesnews.com/politics/new-defence-secretarys-mantra-higher-spending-must-be-matched-faster-modernisation 9] https://www.baesystems.com/en-uk/product/brontanax
text:
As Andy Burnham settles into his role as the new UK Prime Minister, JONATHAN C CLARE, RAeS Head of External Affairs, reviews the new government’s stance for the sector.

With geopolitical instability, accelerating technological competition and renewed industrial policy on the government’s economic agenda, aerospace has shifted from being a sector priority to a strategic national capability. The Burnham government’s first few weeks in office suggest aerospace will play a key role in its ambitions for regional growth, technological leadership and putting the economy on a sound footing.

The new prime minister was quick to champion the aerospace sector with a video address at Farnborough International Airshow (FIA)[1] and attendance of senior cabinet ministers during his first week in leading the government. Ministers appear to be resolute in positioning the aerospace sector front and centre in supporting the UK’s transition to a more productive economy.

The UK’s aerospace, defence, security and space sectors contributed £46.8bn in Gross Value Added (GVA) to the UK economy in 2025, generated almost £110bn in turnover and directly employed 468,500 people[2], demonstrating why successive governments increasingly regard these sectors as strategic national assets.

The new leadership has reaffirmed its commitment to increased defence spending, accelerated investment in artificial intelligence and autonomous systems within its reindustrialisation agenda and promised to use public procurement to support jobs and industrial capability in advanced manufacturing. Luke Pollard who has stayed on as Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry indicated that “record spending on air power, drones and innovation” would help ensure the UK remains at the forefront of defence capability.

A whole-of-government industrial strategy

The government is adopting a more integrated industrial strategy. (Rolls-Royce)

A clear theme emerging from the government’s first few weeks is that aerospace policy is a cross-government endeavour. The government is adopting a more integrated industrial strategy in which HM Treasury, the MoD, UK Space Command, the Department for Business, the Department for Transport and regulator, the Department for Energy Security and regional authorities all contribute towards strengthening national industrial capability. This joined-up approach is vital for the sector.

Jonathan Reynolds, appointed Secretary of State for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, announced a £600m package for British aerospace at the FIA. This included approximately £500m for research and technology projects connected with greener aviation and a £100m supply-chain fund developed with companies and organisations, including Airbus, Rolls-Royce, GKN Aerospace and Safran[3]. Reynolds described aerospace as “one of Britain’s great industrial success stories” and argued that partnerships between business and innovation could harness the country’s “strong manufacturing base and cutting-edge research” while supporting skilled employment across the UK.

The UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT) absorbed the UK Space Agency in April 2026. Despite ministers not calling out the space sector directly, those who visited the Space Zone at FIA signalled ongoing government backing. The government’s approach appears to view space as part of the broader technology ecosystem and a vital strategic capability.

For the Royal Aeronautical Society these announcements indicate that aerospace remains a priority within ministerial portfolios. The test will be whether the government, while speaking the language of reindustrialisation, can move at pace, provide regulatory certainty, investment confidence and long-term policy stability within an industrial sector where investment cycles are measured in decades.

Regional connectivity

Airbus' Wing of Tomorrow programme forms part of a variety of UK aerospace regional clusters. (Airbus)

The new prime minister has promised “good growth in every postcode.” That message has direct relevance for UK aerospace which is distributed across a network of regional clusters. Airbus wing manufacturing at Broughton, Rolls-Royce propulsion expertise in Derby, civil and defence aerospace around Bristol and Filton, rotorcraft in Yeovil, advanced aerostructures in Belfast and space and aerospace activity around Prestwick and Glasgow all demonstrate how national capability is rooted in local ecosystems.

“I’m backing investment and innovation to power good growth in every corner of the UK,” said Jonathan Reynolds, Secretary of State for Business.[4]

For aerospace the government’s focus on devolution should enable further opportunities to move towards stronger regional systems, linking manufacturers, universities, airports, training providers and supply chains. Local institutions may also benefit from greater decision-making over skills funding, infrastructure and investment.

Aerospace for growth

Buying British is a stated aim of the new government. (No.10 Downing Street)

The government interventions and statements so far place aerospace near the front of the government’s industrial programme rather than treating it as a later sectoral priority. Chancellor, John Healey has promised to make every department “a growth department,” with public procurement supporting domestic employment, apprenticeships and skills. His stated objective is “buying British by design,” so that procurement decisions contribute to British investment, innovation and wealth creation. Healey has pointed to his record as Defence Secretary, during which 86% of more than 1,000 major defence contracts went to UK firms[5]. He now intends to extend that direction across government. That said, international defence contractors, including Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Airbus, Thales, Safran, MBDA, Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, Leonardo and other primes continue to support the economy with major UK based operations., will continue to benefit from interwoven supply chains with European and NATO allies as defence procurement and production remains deeply integrated across the alliance. While Europe is investing more heavily in sovereign defence manufacturing, these initiatives should complement rather than replace existing transatlantic industrial partnerships.

Overall, this should all help to strengthen UK supply chains across advanced materials, propulsion, sensors, secure communications, autonomy, digital engineering and mission systems. Procurement reform also offers the possibility of helping innovative SMEs move more rapidly from prototype development into repeat production and export markets.

Defence moves to the centre

The Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and Chief of the Air Staff, ACM Harv Smyth, at the unveiling of BAE Systems' Brontanax CCA. (Tim Robinson/RAeS)

It is evident that defence has shifted to the centre of economic strategy. The composition of the Cabinet reinforces the importance of defence. Ministers have said that keeping the country and its citizens safe is “the first duty of any government.” NATO with unwavering support for the UK’s independent nuclear deterrent underpins the collective defence with the transatlantic alliance. The new Chancellor also reaffirmed that the government intends to meet its international defence commitments, while stressing that “fiscal credibility is the bedrock” of both economic stability and national security.

The government has committed to defence expenditure reaching 3.5% of GDP by 2035. Existing plans provide an additional £15bn for the Defence Investment Plan between 2026-27 and 2029-30[6].

For aerospace more than £8.6bn is to be invested in the Global Combat Air Programme (GCAP) over the next four years, while more than £5bn has been allocated to drones and autonomous systems across the armed forces[7]. The stated objective is to build a more flexible, integrated force and create the ability to “continuously scale production.” This provides substantial opportunities for companies involved in combat air, propulsion, autonomy, mission systems, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence and collaborative combat aircraft (CCAs). It also places pressure on government and industry to demonstrate that increased defence spending produces usable capability rather than slower, more expensive programmes.

Wes Streeting used his first major speech as Defence Secretary to argue that the MoD must make decisions faster, alter its approach to risk and work differently with industry. Defence innovation is frequently constrained not by the absence of technology but by the time required to test, approve, contract and deploy it. Rapid implementation of procurement reform and faster defence acquisitions across departments is urgently needed. Streeting cited the integration of a lower-cost precision weapon onto RAF Typhoons in 42 days[8] as an example of the pace that can be achieved when operational urgency overrides conventional bureaucracy.

The unveiling at Farnborough of BAE Systems’ Brontanax CCA[9], designed and built in Lancashire, is an illustration of the industrial direction. The aircraft is intended to operate alongside crewed fighters, extending sensing and combat reach at a fraction of the cost of a conventional combat aircraft. This is an example in which procurement reform and faster spiral development will determine whether the UK retains technological leadership. BAE's Brontanax is aimed at the RAF Storm Fighter requirement, which will likely see other defence companies look to pitch their CCAs at this highly sought-after prize. Other leading players showcasing CCA platforms include: Airbus (Ravenstorm), Boeing (Ghost Bat), Anduril (Fury) and General Atomics (Gambit).

Technology, sovereignty and dual-use innovation

AI Minister, Kanishka Narayan, said the new prime minister inviting him to attend cabinet as minister for AI was a "sign of his deep commitment to AI's importance." (Siemens)

The newly established Artificial Intelligence Minister, Kanishka Narayan has explained that AI should underpin Britain’s industrial renewal while strengthening national security and public services. For aerospace AI already influences autonomous flight, predictive maintenance, manufacturing inspection, mission planning, digital engineering and air traffic management.

Alongside AI, government priorities now encompass secure semiconductors, cyber resilience, advanced manufacturing, digital engineering and sovereign technology. Aerospace is uniquely positioned as innovation routinely transfers between civil and defence applications. There is a growing demand signal for more dual-use technologies encouraging closer collaboration between government, industry, academia and investors.

Civil aerospace remains central

Scottish airliner, Loganair, purchased electric-powered BETA Alia aircraft during last month's Farnborough International Airshow. (Stephen Bridgewater/RAeS)

Although defence announcements have dominated early ministerial statements, civil aerospace continues to occupy a prominent position within the government’s industrial strategy. Ministerial portfolios remain unchanged for Heidi Alexander, Secretary of State for Transport and Keir Mather, Aviation Minister. The £500m commitment to greener aviation research and technology projects signals continued support for sustainable aviation, advanced propulsion, hydrogen technologies and next-generation manufacturing. Ministers have also recognised the importance of modernising UK airspace, supporting Sustainable Aviation Fuel, encouraging advanced air mobility and improving aviation infrastructure to enable future growth.

The UK continues to possess globally competitive capabilities in aero-engines, wings, aerostructures, systems integration and aerospace research. Maintaining those advantages will require sustained investment that extends beyond research programmes into certification, industrialisation and export growth.

Looking ahead

Volodymyr Zelenskyy become Andy Burnham’s first overseas visitor as prime minister, in a meeting that Burnham said underlined Britain’s support for Ukraine. (No.10 Downing Street)

The government has prioritised the aerospace sector with strategic procurement supporting UK capability, increased defence investment, investment in AI systems and semiconductor resilience, industrial growth, aerospace research and support for the UK supply chain.

However, the government has not yet demonstrated how its spending commitments will be reconciled with the Treasury’s fiscal rules. Questions also remain about how devolved institutions will interact with national aerospace and defence programmes. Furthermore, energy costs, planning reform, engineering skills shortages and access to growth capital remain structural challenges that could limit the return on government investment.

The Royal Aeronautical Society welcomes the government’s recognition that aerospace represents one of the UK’s most strategically important industries.

The alignment of defence, industrial strategy, advanced technology and regional economic growth offers one of the strongest policy environments for aerospace seen in recent years. Ministers have clearly recognised that aerospace contributes not only to exports and high-value employment but also to national resilience and defence, sovereign capability and long-term productivity.

“Our strength lies not just in our fighting power… but in our industrial power too. Investment, growth, jobs and prosperity,” said Lord Coaker, Defence Minister.

Political momentum alone will not sustain aerospace programmes. Success will depend upon stable regulation, long-term investment, competitive energy costs, skilled people, effective institutions and confidence across the investment community. Accelerating initiatives addressing engineering skills, apprenticeships and workforce development in aerospace will be a significant factor.

The new prime minister has committed his government to reindustrialising Britain through innovation and regional growth. Aerospace possesses the industrial depth, scientific capability and export potential to become one of the principal engines of that national renewal.

text:
New Delhi [India], August 6 (ANI): Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu Kinjarapu on Thursday dismissed claims that the government plans to blend ethanol with Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF), calling them 'completely false and irresponsible' after former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal shared a social media post citing a media report on the issue.

In a post on social media, the Civil Aviation Minister said there is no proposal to blend ethanol with ATF and clarified that ethanol and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) are two entirely different fuels.

'The claim that the Government plans to blend ethanol with Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) is completely false and irresponsible. There is no such proposal,' Kinjarapu said.

The Minister further said, 'Ethanol and Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) are entirely different and should not be conflated.'

According to the Minister, 'SAF is an internationally certified aviation fuel recognised by International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO) and adopted globally. It undergoes rigorous testing and meets stringent global safety standards.'

Kinjarapu also cautioned against spreading misinformation on aviation safety, saying such claims only create unnecessary concern among passengers.

'Spreading misinformation on aviation safety only creates needless anxiety among air travellers. Passenger safety remains the Government's highest priority,' he said.

The clarification came after former Delhi Chief Minister Arvind Kejriwal shared a media report on social media and questioned the safety of using what he described as 'adulterated aviation fuel.'

Quoting the report, Kejriwal wrote, 'Read this article. The engine of ur flight just might stop in the air. Will u risk flying in an aircraft running on adulterated aviation fuel? Time to have an educated and competent govt.'

Responding to the remarks, the Civil Aviation Minister reiterated that there is no government proposal to mix ethanol with aviation turbine fuel and stressed that SAF should not be confused with ethanol.

The Minister maintained that Sustainable Aviation Fuel follows internationally accepted certification and safety standards and said passenger safety continues to remain the government's top priority. (ANI)

description:

Long-term demand unlocks Dutch SAF production KLM and SkyNRG have started construction of the Netherlands’ first facility dedicated to sustainable aviation fuel production.

According to KLM, SAF can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by at least 65%.
text:
KLM will purchase at least 75,000 tonnes of sustainable aviation fuel each year, equal to 75% of the plant’s output.

The long-term agreement represents a sustainability commitment of nearly $3.5 billion and helped SkyNRG secure project financing.

Production is expected to begin in 2028 as the Netherlands works toward its national target of 14% SAF use by 2030.

Long-term demand unlocks Dutch SAF production

KLM and SkyNRG have started construction of the Netherlands’ first facility dedicated to sustainable aviation fuel production.

The SkyNRG Delfzijl plant, known as DSL-01, is expected to begin producing fuel in 2028. Once operational, it will supply about 100,000 tonnes of SAF each year.

KLM has committed to purchasing at least 75,000 tonnes annually. That represents 75% of the facility’s planned SAF output and nearly $3.5 billion in long-term spending.

The agreement gives SkyNRG a large, committed customer before production begins. Such contracts are crucial for capital-intensive climate infrastructure. They provide revenue certainty and help developers secure financing.

KLM co-founded SkyNRG in 2009 and has supported the development of the SAF market since then. Its long-term purchase commitment directly contributed to the financing and development of the Delfzijl project.

“As the first airline in the world, our long-term offtake agreement directly contributes to the financing and realization of this facility. Today, together with SkyNRG and other invited guests, we mark a milestone by celebrating the start of construction, making this project finally tangible. I am proud that KLM, as a co-founder of SkyNRG and the largest purchaser of the fuel, is taking an important step in scaling up SAF production in the Netherlands and further advancing the sustainability of aviation,” said Marjan Rintel, CEO of KLM.

SAF offers deep cuts in lifecycle emissions

Aviation remains difficult to decarbonize because long-distance aircraft still depend on energy-dense liquid fuels. Battery and hydrogen technologies are unlikely to replace conventional jet fuel across major international routes in the near term.

SAF can work within existing aircraft and fuel infrastructure. However, its climate value depends on the feedstocks, production process and energy used.

The fuel releases carbon dioxide during flight, much like fossil kerosene. Its overall lifecycle emissions can be substantially lower because the carbon comes from renewable or recycled sources.

According to KLM, SAF can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by at least 65%. Some production pathways can deliver reductions above 90% compared with conventional kerosene.

RELATED ARTICLE: KLM and ZeroAvia to Launch Zero-Emission Hydrogen Flight by 2026

“Today’s milestone in Delfzijl shows that large-scale SAF production in the Netherlands is becoming a reality. We are proud to take this step together with KLM and our partners, whose long-term commitment has helped make this project possible. DSL-01 is an important step toward scaling SAF production and accelerating the transition to more sustainable aviation,” said Maarten van Dijk, CEO of SkyNRG.

Cost gap remains a barrier to wider adoption

Despite its emissions benefits, SAF remains three to four times more expensive than fossil kerosene. Limited production capacity, feedstock constraints and high development costs continue to restrict supply.

That price gap creates financial pressure for airlines operating on narrow margins. It also raises questions about how the transition will affect ticket prices, competitiveness and demand.

KLM is calling for stronger government support to expand production and reduce costs. The airline has proposed a national SAF fund, following recommendations in the Wennink report, “The Route to Future Prosperity.”

The Netherlands has set a national ambition of reaching 14% SAF use by 2030. By comparison, European rules require fuel supplied at covered EU airports to contain at least 6% SAF from 2030.

The new Dutch coalition agreement includes plans to expand alternative aviation fuels and support domestic production. The challenge will be converting those commitments into bankable incentives without weakening sustainability standards.

For executives and investors, DSL-01 shows how long-term corporate purchasing can unlock industrial decarbonization projects. It also exposes the limits of voluntary action.

One plant will not provide enough fuel to transform Dutch aviation. Replicating the model will require coordinated policy, reliable demand and substantial private capital. The Netherlands’ success could influence how other aviation hubs finance the next generation of low-carbon fuel infrastructure.

text:
The Senate Agriculture Committee on Aug. 6 failed to advance the Agricultural Act of 2026, commonly referred to as the Farm Bill. Committee members are expected to continue work on the legislation when the Senate reconvenes in mid-September.

The legislation stalled due to partisan divisions over food assistance provisions, with committee members voting 10-11 against advancing the bill to the full Senate. Committee Chairman John Boozman, R-Ark., recessed the committee rather than adjuring the committee, which means he can call committee members back to revisit the bill at a later date. The Senate is scheduled to be in recess Aug. 10 through mid-September, officially returning to legislative session on Sept. 14. Committee members are expected to resume work on the Farm Bill soon after that time.

One provision of the Senate Farm Bill would enable year-round sales of E15 and implement reform to the Renewable Fuel Standard’s small refinery exemption (SRE) program. Prior to the committee’s Aug. 6 vote, both Boozeman and Ranking Member Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., expressed strong support for the bill’s E15 language.

“Thanks to the efforts of Senators Fischer, Thune, Capito, and Daines we have included year-round E15,” Boozeman said. “Today, Senators will have an opportunity for the first time to advance out of committee, legislation that will authorize the blending of E15 year-round.”

“I am committed to continuing to work with Chairman Boozman on this bill to get it done and there are good things in it for our farmers and ranchers, including year-round E-15, a provision I have long led on,” Klobuchar said.

In addition to E15 and SRE reform, the Senate Farm Bill’s energy title includes numerous provisions to support the U.S. biofuel industry, including major updates to the USDA’s Section 9003 loan guarantee program, language supporting the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) industry, and the reauthorizes of numerous bioenergy programs, including the Bioenergy Program for Advanced Biofuels, Biodiesel Fuel Education Program, Feedstock Flexibility Program for Bioenergy Producers, the Biomass Crop Assistance Program, and the Carbon Utilization and Biogas Education Program.

National Sorghum Producers is calling on the committee to continue work on the Farm Bill. “We are disappointed that the committee failed to advance legislation important to farmers and rural America,” said Amy France, chair of NSP and a sorghum farmer from Scott City, Kansas. “Especially at a time when producers are facing weak prices, high costs and continued uncertainty.

“We urge senators in both parties to return to the table as soon as possible.,” France continued. “Congress needs to deliver a bipartisan farm bill that provides farmers certainty, expands markets through year-round E15 and preserves Sen. Moran’s Food for Peace amendment.”

The National Corn Growers Association is urging the committee to take action on the Farm Bill as soon as possible. “We are extremely disappointed that legislation important to so many Americans failed to advance,” said Jed Bower, president of the NCGA. “This bill was particularly important to corn growers who have long pushed for legislation that would allow for the year-round sale of E15, a bright spot in an otherwise dim economic outlook.

“We implore senators to approve a bipartisan farm bill that extends consumer access to E15 and serves the interests of America’s farmers,” Bower continued. “We are running out of time in this Congress and urge action as quickly as possible.”

The Minnesota Bio-Fuels Association stressed the urgent need to pass E15 legislation. “Today’s outcome on the Senate Farm Bill is a missed opportunity for drivers, farmers, fuel retailers and rural communities that need certainty,” said Brian Werner, executive director of MN Bio-Fuels.

“Year-round E15 is not controversial. Minnesotans want lower-cost fuel choices, stronger markets for farmers and more access to homegrown energy,” he added. “Delaying action keeps outdated restrictions in place and limits access to a fuel option that overwhelmingly benefits consumers, agriculture and rural communities.

“The Senate Agriculture Committee did not reject year-round E15,” Werner continued. “They failed to pass a bipartisan Farm Bill over an unrelated disagreement on SNAP. We thank Senators Klobuchar and Smith for their supportive statements and we will continue working with lawmakers to make year-round E15 permanent.”

text:
Sagepoint Logistics, a subsidiary of Sagepoint Energy, announced on Aug. 5 it has closed a senior secured financing with Power Sustainable Infrastructure Credit Manager L.P. (PSIC) to expand its dedicated truckload carrier fueled by renewable natural gas (RNG). The financing funds the acquisition of a dedicated fleet of 60 Class 8 heavy-duty trucks and related fueling infrastructure, building on Sagepoint’s capabilities in renewable natural gas (RNG).

Through this investment, Sagepoint Logistics extends the company’s operations downstream from RNG production and dispensing into end-use transportation, creating a more integrated pathway from waste-derived fuel production to end use. This integration translates into three key benefits for Sagepoint Logistics’ customers: greater cost stability, measurable scope 3 emissions reductions, and a carrier with the ability to scale.

Unlike most carriers that are subject to the volatility of diesel fuel markets, Sagepoint Logistics is uniquely positioned to offer customers greater cost stability. Powered by renewable natural gas (RNG) produced by Sagepoint Energy’s own facilities, the fleet operates on a vertically integrated fuel supply that helps insulate customers from fluctuating fuel costs and provides a more predictable transportation cost structure. Equipped with Cummins’ X15N natural gas engines, purpose-built for heavy-duty, long-haul Class 8 applications, the fleet delivers the performance customers expect while running on RNG. For shippers focused on reducing emissions across their supply chain, partnering with Sagepoint Logistics provides a practical way to lower Scope 3 emissions without compromising on cost efficiency or performance.

The initial fleet operates throughout the Midwest from Sagepoint Logistics’ Green Bay, WI hub, and the PSIC facility provides additional capacity to expand the fleet and broaden its geographic footprint over time. This scalable model enables shippers to increase freight volumes with a carrier built to meet their evolving transportation needs.

As customer demand grows, Sagepoint Logistics is also investing in the communities it serves by expanding its workforce and strengthening the local economy, while increasing its capacity to serve more customers. In addition, the fleet’s use of RNG instead of diesel helps reduce emissions, supporting a more sustainable transportation network in communities across the Midwest.

“Most carriers buy their fuel. We make ours,” said Aaron Johnson, CEO of Sagepoint Energy. “That’s the difference for our customers: cost stability that comes from controlling our own fuel supply, a real reduction in Scope 3 emissions, and a fleet that can grow at the same pace they do. This financing with PSIC gives us the capital to connect our RNG production directly to end-use transportation and scale that offering over time.”

“We are pleased to expand our partnership with Sagepoint as the company extends its capabilities from RNG production and dispensing into transportation,” said Daniel Fein, managing director of PSIC. “Sagepoint Logistics creates an integrated source of end-use demand for RNG while providing commercial customers with a practical pathway to reduce emissions relative to conventional diesel-powered transportation. This transaction reflects our strategy of providing tailored capital to infrastructure businesses with strong underlying assets, experienced management teams and identifiable growth opportunities.”

Haynes and Boone, LLP served as legal counsel to PSIC. Moore & Van Allen served as legal counsel to Sagepoint.

text:
Electrofuels made from captured carbon dioxide and renewable electricity have powered a scheduled U.S. commercial passenger flight after moving through a conventional airport fuel network for the first time. The demonstration marks a key milestone for power-to-liquids technology, showing that synthetic aviation fuel can integrate with today’s fueling infrastructure without requiring changes to aircraft or airport operations.

American Airlines operated the flight from Corpus Christi International Airport to Dallas Fort Worth International Airport using electro-sustainable aviation fuel (eSAF) produced by clean fuels developer Infinium. The fuel reached the aircraft through the airport’s existing fuel system, providing a real-world demonstration of next-generation aviation fuel technology.

Power-to-liquids takes flight

Unlike conventional sustainable aviation fuels that rely on biological feedstocks, Infinium’s eSAF uses waste carbon dioxide and renewable electricity. The process combines captured carbon with hydrogen produced using renewable power to create synthetic hydrocarbons that closely resemble conventional jet fuel.

The fuel came from Infinium’s Pathfinder facility in Corpus Christi, the world’s first commercial-scale power-to-liquids eFuels plant. Operating since 2023, the site initially produced eDiesel and eNaphtha before expanding into sustainable aviation fuel. According to the company, its production process can reduce lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by more than 90% compared with conventional petroleum-based jet fuel.

More from Transportation

See All

Infinium CEO Robert Schuetzle said the company has already proven commercial production of low-carbon fuels for trucking and industrial uses. He said adding eSAF to the product lineup and powering a passenger flight represents another step toward wider commercial adoption.

Fits today’s infrastructure

The engineering milestone extends beyond the fuel itself. Engineers blended the synthetic fuel with conventional Jet A before confirming it met ASTM International fuel specifications for commercial aviation.

The certified blend entered Corpus Christi International Airport’s shared fuel storage system before American Airlines allocated it to a scheduled passenger flight. Airport infrastructure, fueling equipment and aircraft engines required no modifications, demonstrating that eSAF can function as a drop-in replacement within existing aviation fuel networks.

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom said the flight shows how emerging fuel technologies can move from demonstration projects into commercial operations. He added that expanding production at lower costs will remain critical for reducing aviation emissions.

Scaling synthetic fuel

Commercial aviation consumes nearly 100 billion gallons of jet fuel every year, yet sustainable aviation fuel still accounts for less than 1% of global supply. Electrofuels have gained attention because they avoid biological feedstocks while fitting into existing distribution systems.

Infinium plans to expand production through its Project Roadrunner facility, which is under construction and expected to begin producing eSAF in 2027. Once fully operational, the plant is projected to produce more than 5 million gallons annually.

The successful deployment suggests one of the biggest technical hurdles has already been cleared. Power-to-liquids fuel can move through today’s aviation supply chain and power existing aircraft. The industry’s next challenge will be scaling production quickly enough to supply airlines at commercially viable costs.

text:
Fort Worth-based American Airlines has flown what it says is the first U.S. commercial passenger flight to use synthetic jet fuel made from waste carbon dioxide and renewable electricity, delivered through a commercial airport’s fuel system. The flight landed at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport.

The electro sustainable aviation fuel, or eSAF, came from California-based Infinium’s Pathfinder facility in Corpus Christi. American and Infinium said the batch represented the first delivery of sustainable aviation fuel made without biobased feedstocks to a commercial airport in the United States.

“This flight represents a significant moment for aviation,” American CEO Robert Isom said in a statement. “Through our partnership with Infinium, we’re demonstrating how next generation technologies like eSAF can move from early investment to real-world application. Scaling SAF production at lower prices is essential to reducing emissions, strengthening our long-term competitiveness, and continuing to deliver the connectivity and economic benefits that our customers rely on.”

How the fuel reached the airplane

Infinium describes Pathfinder as the world’s first commercial-scale power-to-liquids eFuels production site. The batch was blended with conventional jet fuel. It then was tested against the ASTM International specification for Jet A, certifying it for use in today’s aircraft engines and fueling infrastructure without modification. It was then delivered into the common jet fuel tanks at Corpus Christi International Airport and allocated to the American flight bound for DFW.

Infinium said its eSAF can cut lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions by more than 90% compared with conventional petroleum-based jet fuel while moving through the same pipelines, tanks and fueling equipment airlines already use.

“Adding eSAF to our product slate — and seeing it power a commercial passenger flight — marks another meaningful step forward in bringing practical, low-carbon fuel solutions to industry,” Infinium CEO Robert Schuetzle said in a statement.

Bigger plant due in 2027

American holds an offtake agreement for commercial volumes of eSAF from Infinium’s Project Roadrunner, a larger power-to-liquids plant now under construction. The offtake is supported in part by a separate agreement with Citi to enable Scope 3 emissions reductions from employee travel. Breakthrough Energy Catalyst and Brookfield Asset Management are financing the project, with nonrecourse project debt from HSBC. Production and deliveries are expected to begin in 2027. Once it reaches full capacity, Project Roadrunner is expected to produce more than 5 million gallons of eSAF a year.

“This first-of-its-kind eSAF flight from American Airlines and Infinium is an important step for lower carbon aviation and we are proud to support this effort with our long-time partner,” Citi Head of Enterprise Services and Public Affairs Edward Skyler said in a statement. “Given the potential SAF has on reducing emissions, we look forward to efforts to scale its production.”

Where things stand with sustainable aviation fuel

Aviation consumes nearly 100 billion gallons of jet fuel a year, and global air travel exceeds 4 billion passengers annually. Sustainable aviation fuel accounts for less than 1% of jet fuel used worldwide, the companies said.

The Infinium flight comes two months after American and Google signed what the companies called a record-breaking sustainable aviation fuel certificate agreement. That agreement covers 35 million gallons over three years, with the physical fuel going to Chicago O’Hare International Airport.

In April, Infinium’s Project Atlas was selected to supply fuel under the Sustainable Aviation Buyers Alliance’s next-generation procurement. American serves as the end-use airline in what Infinium called its second eSAF agreement with the carrier.

American is also a cornerstone investor, alongside Alaska Airlines, in the $150 million sustainable aviation fuels fund launched by Fort Worth-based oneworld alliance with Breakthrough Energy Ventures.

title: Toxic underground fires are spreading at California landfills - Los Angeles Times
description:
Three years ago, environmental regulators discovered garbage burning deep inside the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in the Santa Clarita Valley.
At first, local officials described the problem in Los Angeles County at Chiquita Canyon landfill as a rare, even unprecedented disaster.
But since then, California regulators have learned that at least two other landfills are wrestling with high temperatures and similar conditions.
Schiavo said the stench near Chiquita Canyon has gotten worse in recent days as workers try to stabilize the hillside.
In other air pollution news Wildfires have scorched thousands of acres in Washington state.
text:
Three years ago, environmental regulators discovered garbage burning deep inside the Chiquita Canyon Landfill in the Santa Clarita Valley. Few imagined the calamity that would follow.

Somehow the landfill’s pollution control system introduced oxygen below, causing decades-old waste to rapidly decompose, generating intense heat and eventually widespread smoldering, federal and state environmental agencies say. The broiling temperatures released toxic gases and hazardous liquid waste that bubbled up to the surface. Residents living in the nearby communities of Val Verde and Castaic have phoned in thousands of complaints about stench and lived with nausea, dizziness and trouble breathing.

The underground fire has tripled in size since first confirmed in 2023. Recently a towering mound of landfill garbage perched on the hillside has warped and threatens to trigger an avalanche of garbage and chemical-filled liquid, or leachate, according to the California water board. Waste Connections, the landfill’s owner and operator, says it has been working to stabilize that area.

“In a worst case scenario, the hillside can liquefy and actually slide into the community,” Assemblymember Pilar Schiavo (D-Santa Clarita) said at a news conference last month.

At first, local officials described the problem in Los Angeles County at Chiquita Canyon landfill as a rare, even unprecedented disaster. But since then, California regulators have learned that at least two other landfills are wrestling with high temperatures and similar conditions.

Scorching temperatures have overtaken at least 30 acres of El Sobrante landfill near Corona in Riverside County. Excessive heat and emissions have also been detected at Avenal landfill in the San Joaquin Valley.

The discoveries raise an unsettling question: How many landfills are dealing with these disasters? Are they a broader problem in California?

If you live near a landfill and have experienced an abnormal spike in odors or other issues, we would appreciate the opportunity to hear about your experience.

At Chiquita Canyon, conditions have continued to deteriorate.

In the years that I’ve covered this issue, I’ve met residents who’ve taken extreme measures to escape the toxic pollution. They’ve worn gas masks and slept overnight in grocery store parking lots. Several families sold their homes.

Those who have stayed continue to deal with risks to their health and safety. Schiavo said the stench near Chiquita Canyon has gotten worse in recent days as workers try to stabilize the hillside.

In Val Verde, children out of school for the summer have hardly been able to enjoy their time off.

“They are already suffering — prisoners in their own homes,” Schiavo said. “They have a great trampoline in front of their house. They can’t jump around on because of this toxic air.”

On a recent weekday morning, landfill workers were staged around the damaged, western side of the landfill with heavy machinery. Across the street, dozens Los Angeles County firefighter recruits jogged at the Del Valle Regional Training Center, pushing through the inescapable aroma of trash in the air.

Abigail DeSesa, a longtime resident of Val Verde who lives about a mile from Chiquita Canyon, said she regularly wakes up with pounding headaches she believes are related to landfill gases from the fire. She’s gone to a community relief center set up at a local hotel to escape the smell, but has to return home at the end of the day.

“The gas is getting into our homes and I am waking up sick every morning,” DeSesa said. “Where is the relief for that? I did not break the landfill, so why am I paying a heavy price with my physical and mental health to fix it?”

Chiquita Canyon closed at the end of the 2024 and stopped accepting new garbage. But the fire is expected to last for years as it continues to consume decades-old trash.

Underground landfill fires are complex, nearly impossible to extinguish once they break out. As regulators search for a solution, residents are really struggling with the wait.

In other air pollution news

Wildfires have scorched thousands of acres in Washington state. They’ve destroyed hundreds of homes, prompting tens of thousands of people to evacuate and filling the air with black smoke. For some, the disaster is reminiscent of the 2025 wildfires in Southern California, L.A. Times reporter Clara Harter wrote.

Wildfire smoke has overwhelmed large swathes of the Pacific Northwest, reaching hazardous levels in areas closest to active blazes. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration observed a large plume of smoke extending southward over the Pacific Ocean. The pollution is expected to drift into the Bay Area, stealthily diminishing air quality without the signature campfire smell associated with wildfire smoke, according to Anthony Edwards, the San Francisco Chronicle’s newsroom meteorologist.

In-N-Out, a the beloved California fast food chain, recently found itself at the center of heated debate in Culver City. Are the restaurant’s popular burgers worth the added traffic and air pollution? L.A. Times business reporter Suhauna Husain writes that some residents are fiercely opposed to a proposed In-N-Out in Culver City, arguing the chain’s notoriously congested drive-throughs — filled with idling cars — could pose a health and safety risk. The Culver City Council responded by extending its moratorium on new drive-through restaurants.

Other environmental news

Wildfire seasons are becoming alarmingly more destructive in California, and they’re erasing a commodity already in short supply — housing. At the turn of the century, wildfire destroyed about 3% of the California homes they came into contact with, per L.A. Times wildfire reporter Noah Haggarty. The rate rose to 18% by 2020 — despite extensive home-hardening practices.

The aviation industry is exploring using a Brazilian palm tree to make jet fuel. Researchers say oil-rich macauba palm seeds can be harvested to make a cleaner and renewable source of aviation fuel, Bloomberg energy correspondent Peter Millard reports. Aviation emissions have been increasing globally, prompting some governments to pursue alternatives to fossil fuels. Although sustainable aviation fuel is very small segment of the market, European mandates may drive airlines to seek out reliable sources in the near future.

Small farmers claim they are being harmed by California groundwater regulations, causing some to leave more land fallow, according to L.A. Times water reporter Ian James. The strict fee structure and complex rules were designed to prevent overpumping and aquifer depletion. But these “one-size-fit-all” regulations impose a greater financial burden on small farmers — that generally use less water.

text:
The Lula administration is considering including in regulations governing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) a mechanism that would allow international airlines to purchase environmental certificates generated by the fuels to help meet their decarbonization targets.

Airlines face sustainable fuel rollout amid supply concerns

Agriculture could export R$2bn in carbon credits

The proposal is intended to make Brazilian SAF more competitive, Marlon Arraes, acting national secretary for Oil, Natural Gas and Biofuels at the Ministry of Mines and Energy (MME), said Wednesday during a debate hosted by the American Chamber of Commerce for Brazil (Amcham) as part of São Paulo Climate Week.

The discussion is part of efforts to regulate the National Sustainable Aviation Fuel Program (ProBioQAV), established under the Future Fuels Law. ProBioQAV requires Brazilian airlines to reduce their carbon emissions starting next year, initially by 1%. The plan is to encourage SAF production and use to meet the targets.

Currently, only Petrobras has the capacity to produce lower-emission aviation fuel through the coprocessing of renewable feedstocks with oil products. The state-run company has already used corn and soybean oils. Even once dedicated SAF plants come online, it will not be possible to physically separate the renewable portion of the fuel from the fossil-based portion. Airlines will therefore need to purchase SAF Sustainability Certificates (CSSAFs) to demonstrate compliance with their targets. The regulations now under discussion are expected to establish rules governing the issuance and trading of CSSAFs.

The proposal would allow the CSSAF trading infrastructure to include foreign participants. “We are working to enable ‘book-and-claim’ mechanisms so that sectors in other countries can finance this decarbonization and make our product competitive,” Arraes said during the debate. Under a book-and-claim system, companies pay for environmental attributes to demonstrate compliance with their emissions targets, without having to physically receive the associated fuel.

Government officials are also discussing whether Brazilian airlines should be allowed to sell these certificates to international carriers, which will also face emissions-reduction targets starting in 2027 under the International Civil Aviation Organization’s (ICAO) decarbonization program.

“Studies show that Brazil could become a provider of this SAF solution. What we need to do is establish a regulatory framework for meeting the national target that provides for this type of mechanism,” Arraes said.

text:
Aether Fuels, a climate technology company developing scalable, economical sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and sustainable liquid hydrocarbons, today announced the formation of its inaugural Advisory Board, bringing together five distinguished leaders whose expertise spans aviation, energy, climate policy, finance, project development, and corporate strategy.

The establishment of the Advisory Board marks an important milestone for Aether as the company advances the commercialisation of its proprietary Aurora™ technology platform and continues developing commercial projects globally, including Project Beacon. The Advisory Board will provide strategic guidance as Aether expands industry partnerships, advances project development, and brings next-generation sustainable fuel production to the market.

"Aether has reached an exciting point in our journey," said Conor Madigan, Co-Founder and CEO of Aether Fuels. "Over the past several years, we've demonstrated our technology at pilot and demo scale, built a world-class team, and established commercial partnerships that position us for long-term growth. As we transition into commercial deployment, the guidance of experienced leaders who have built global energy businesses, shaped climate policy, financed major projects, and transformed the aviation industry will be invaluable. We're honored to welcome these exceptional advisors as we continue building the future of sustainable fuels."

Advisory Board Members

David Hone is a climate and energy expert with more than 40 years of experience in the oil and gas industry. He serves as Chief Climate Change Adviser at Shell International and works within Shell's scenarios team, where he focuses on climate strategy, energy transition pathways, and the practical implementation of decarbonization solutions. Earlier in his career, he worked as a refinery engineer in Australia and the Netherlands, then moved into oil trading in London, where he held several senior roles before taking on his climate advisory position in 2001. He has also served as a board member of the Global Carbon Capture and Storage Institute, previously served as a board member of the Centre for Climate and Energy Solutions, and served as Chairman of the International Emissions Trading Association from 2011 to 2013. He is also the author of Putting the Genie Back: Solving the Climate and Energy Dilemma.

David G. Victor is Professor of Innovation and Public Policy at the University of California San Diego, Co-Director of the UC San Diego Initiative on Deep Decarbonization, and Director of the Scripps Institution of Oceanography's Carbon Removal Initiative. His work sits at the intersection of climate policy, energy systems, and the political economy of decarbonization, with a focus on how emissions reductions can be achieved in the real world where economic and political constraints matter. Before joining UC San Diego, he served as Professor of Law at Stanford Law School and directed Stanford’s Program on Energy and Sustainable Development. Over the course of his career, he has advised a wide range of organisations including BP, Chevron, Duke Energy, the World Bank, the OECD, and multiple United Nations bodies. He is also one of the most widely published voices in climate policy, with books including Fixing the Climate, Making Climate Policy Work, and Global Warming Gridlock.

Lina Lee is a global energy, finance, and strategy executive with more than 25 years of leadership experience across petrochemicals, trading, treasury, and corporate development. She previously served as CFO & VP Strategy for BP’s Global Petrochemicals business, where she led strategic transformation, risk management, and digital initiatives designed to improve resilience and operational performance. Her career at BP also included senior roles in strategy, commercial development, and operational excellence, as well as serving as Chief Executive of Trading & Shipping for BP China. Earlier in her career, she held finance roles at Bank of America Merrill Lynch and Air Products. Today, she serves as an Independent Non-Executive Director at Valeura Energy, where she sits on the Audit & Risk Committee and the Governance, Nomination & Compensation Committee, and brings deep experience in governance, cross-border growth strategy, and navigating the energy transition across global markets.

Sheila Remes retired in April 2024 as Vice President of Environmental Sustainability at The Boeing Company, capping a 30-year career with one of the world’s leading aerospace companies. During her time at Boeing, she held a range of leadership roles spanning environmental sustainability, strategy, commercial airplanes, marketing, sales, and engineering, including serving as Vice President of Strategy for Boeing Commercial Airplanes. Prior to Boeing, she also spent 10 years in the airline industry, with experience at America West supporting the technical side of operations as an engineer and at United supporting the commercial side of the business. She currently serves on the boards of the World Affairs Council of Seattle and Forest Ridge of the Sacred Heart School, and on the advisory boards of the International Aviation Women’s Association and the UCLA Institute for Carbon Management. Her work today continues to focus on sustainable aviation, leadership development, and supporting women and girls pursuing STEM careers.

Eric (Ric) Redman Transitions to Advisory Board

Effective September 1, 2026, Eric (Ric) Redman will also join Aether's Advisory Board, transitioning from his executive leadership role after four years helping guide the company through its early formative years.

Since joining Aether, Redman has played an integral role in shaping the company's corporate strategy, government affairs, and project development efforts. His leadership has helped position Aether for its current phase of commercialization.

Redman brings more than 40 years of experience across the energy, electric power, environmental, and renewable energy sectors. Throughout his career, he has led the development of more than 8 GW of renewable energy and state-of-the-art power projects across North America and has been a pioneer in renewable energy policy, carbon capture and sequestration, and clean energy project development. He holds a J.D. from Harvard Law School, an M.A. from Oxford University as a Rhodes Scholar, and has built a career at the intersection of business, policy, and the energy transition.

His transition to the Advisory Board reflects both the evolution of Aether's organization and the company's continued growth.

"Ric has been instrumental in helping build Aether from its earliest days," said Madigan. "His strategic insight, policy expertise, and unwavering commitment to our mission have shaped the company we are today. We're excited that he'll continue supporting Aether as an advisor going forward."

Collectively, the Advisory Board's experience spans every major discipline required to commercialize next-generation sustainable fuels, including aviation, refining, climate policy, project finance, corporate strategy, and global energy markets. Their expertise will support Aether as it advances commercial deployment of the Aurora™ technology platform and continues building strategic partnerships across the sustainable aviation fuel value chain.

title: Healthy Forests Need Healthy Markets - Forest Resources Association
description:
Today, as more markets have disappeared or weakened, one truth has become increasingly clear: healthy forests depend on healthy markets.
The loss of wood markets has become a growing concern for foresters, loggers, landowners, and policymakers.
For more on Markets Matter initiatives, register for FRA’s August webinar, Markets Matter: From Convening to Action — Join Us in Building the Markets Our Forests Need.
Healthy forests need healthy markets.
Each of us has a role to play in supporting the markets, partnerships, and innovation needed to sustain both healthy forests and a strong forest products industry.
text:
My first forestry job was a summer position with a small consulting firm in northwest Wisconsin in 2006. I helped set up timber sales for small private woodland owners and, as an eager but inexperienced forester, learned the basics of navigation, tree identification, silviculture, property lines, and harvest boundaries. One thing I do not remember worrying about was whether there would be a market for the stumpage we were selling. At the time, it seemed that every species that met the minimum diameter threshold had a home. That confidence has changed. Today, as more markets have disappeared or weakened, one truth has become increasingly clear: healthy forests depend on healthy markets.

The loss of wood markets has become a growing concern for foresters, loggers, landowners, and policymakers. As timber markets decline, forest management activities needed to improve wildlife habitat, reduce wildfire and forest health risks, and ensure future timber resources become increasingly difficult to carry out. Consider a forester working with a private landowner, perhaps under Wisconsin’s Managed Forest Law (MFL)—the state’s tax incentive program for sustainable forest management—or a public agency managing a stand scheduled for treatment. The stand may be overcrowded and require thinning to improve its health and vigor. It may have invasive species concerns, lack desirable regeneration, or require the removal of lower-quality trees to improve wildlife habitat and create growing space for healthier species. From a forest management perspective, the prescription may be sound, but whether it can be implemented often depends on having a viable market for the wood removed during the treatment.

Many trees selected for removal in these treatments are not high-value sawlogs or meet pulpwood specifications of local mills. They may be better suited for chips, biomass, pallet material, or other lower-value products. As markets have waned, low-grade markets have often been hit hardest. Without a market for those products, harvest economics quickly become more difficult. The combined costs of setup, harvesting, trucking, and processing can exceed the wood’s value across the supply chain. That pressure is increasingly visible across the Lake States. Weak pulp markets, oversupplied hardwood markets, housing-related slowdowns affecting lumber demand, volatile mill purchasing patterns, and significant mill closures have created ripple effects for loggers, truckers, contractors, landowners, and mills. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources has noted that while harvestable timber remains available on the landscape, many landowners now struggle to find logging contractors and viable markets for certain wood products. Market conditions and changing demand continue to shape which forest management activities can realistically occur. This highlights a reality that wasn’t always such a concern. Sustainable forestry is not just a science-based system; it is also an economic system.

As we all understand, the forest products industry supports thousands of jobs and generates significant dollars in product output. Trees are harvested through responsible forest management into products people use every day. Every sawmill, pulp or paper mill, mat facility, pellet facility, pallet manufacturer, pole processing plant, and specialty wood products company provides benefits to society and helps keep forests manageable. Each lost market creates ripple effects throughout the supply chain, reaching all the way back to the forest. When markets exist at scale for low-grade wood, foresters can implement silvicultural treatments that improve stand quality, landowners can afford needed treatments, logging contractors can keep operating, and mills can secure raw material, and we all benefit from the healthy forests, wildlife habitat, and products they produce. The result is healthier forests and stronger rural economies. As those markets decline, management opportunities decline with them.

One of the best parts of working in the forest products industry is seeing the resilience of the people in it. Industry leaders, government agencies, educational institutions, and stakeholder organizations like FRA are actively working to address today’s market challenges. The Wisconsin Forests FIRST initiative is one example of this work in action. It focuses attention on the connection between sustainable forestry, forest products manufacturing, workforce development, and economic growth. Efforts like this recognize that healthy forests require the infrastructure and markets that support active forest management (For an in-depth update on the Wisconsin Forests FIRST initiative, consider attending the FRA Fall Meeting in Green Bay, Wisconsin, September 30–October 1).

The Lake States remain fortunate to have abundant forest resources, a strong manufacturing base, and a long tradition of sustainable forest management. Existing forest product markets are essential to keeping sustainable forest management economically viable. However, as traditional markets have declined, the need to develop new outlets for harvested wood and residuals must be explored. New opportunities for underutilized wood resources which could complement traditional markets have emerged, including mass timber, wood pellets, bioenergy, biochar, and potentially woody biomass as a feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel. These emerging markets could create additional outlets for lower-value wood, improve forest health and productivity, and strengthen the economic foundation needed to support future forest management and the broader supply chain. Success will require continued collaboration and consensus on the best path forward to maintain the viability of existing mills while attracting new mills where resources are underutilized. That message was central to the recent Markets Matter Convening in Madison, Wisconsin, where participants from across the forest products supply chain discussed the need to maintain and expand markets for sustainably produced wood. The event reinforced a reality familiar to forestry professionals and highlighted the need for collaboration to support the industry’s future. For more on Markets Matter initiatives, register for FRA’s August webinar, Markets Matter: From Convening to Action — Join Us in Building the Markets Our Forests Need.

Healthy forests need healthy markets. Without strong, reliable outlets for wood, especially lower-value material, the management options needed to keep forests healthy can become limited or disappear altogether. The forest products industry is meeting these challenges head-on through initiatives such as Wisconsin Forests FIRST, Markets Matter, and other collaborative efforts across the supply chain. Each of us has a role to play in supporting the markets, partnerships, and innovation needed to sustain both healthy forests and a strong forest products industry.
